title: edf reports 87 drop first half profits 2026 07 31
text:
PARIS, July 31 (Reuters) - French state-owned utility EDF advised on Friday that full-year earnings before interest, tax, depreciation and amortisation (EBITDA) for 2026 were expected to ​fall by 10% compared to last year as low market prices continue to ‌weigh on the utility's profits and successive heatwaves reduced power output.
France's dominant power producer EDF grappled with successive heatwaves this summer that saw temperatures go to over 40 degrees Celsius, curtailing power at nuclear plants and ​causing record drought and wildfires across the country.
EDF Chief Executive Bernard Fontana said that the ​long shutdown at the Chooz 2 nuclear reactor in northern France due ⁠to low river levels, and outage at the Golfech 2 reactor due to high river ​temperatures, were expected to weigh on full year-profits.
The heatwave and lack of rain also caused slightly ​lower water levels for hydroelectric plants, he said.
EDF is working on adapting its nuclear fleet for higher and hotter temperatures over the coming decade with €8.7 billion earmarked for adaptations across their nuclear fleet, hydroelectric plants and ​grid assets.
"It can cause some arbitrage on the budget so some may be tempted to ​put it off but we keep the discipline as it is good for the country," Fontana said.
At the ‌height ⁠of the heatwave over 9 gigawatts of total capacity was reduced across twelve reactors, or roughly 15% of the 57-reactor fleet, Kpler data showed. EDF also reported an 8.7% drop in first-half net income, impacted by lower wholesale electricity prices. This marks the second consecutive year of lower earnings due to falling ​market prices. European power prices ​hit their lowest ⁠level since the start of the Covid pandemic in January 2026 and have only partially rebounded compared to the first half of 2025. EDF sells ​power several years in advance, so recent price lows are only ​starting to reflect ⁠on its balance sheet. The state-owned group is also embarking on a massive investment programme expected to cost over half a trillion euros to renovate its power grid and nuclear fleet. Around 70 ⁠billion euros ​are earmarked for the development of six nuclear reactors, ​with the first expected to be online by 2038.
